title: Ibrahim, an example
hook: in Ibrahim and those with him is an excellent example (60:4)
tomorrow: Kindness to those who don't fight you

segments.voice: Yesterday: the end of Surah Al-Hashr, name after name for God. Your line was his are the beautiful names. Today, Surah sixty, She who is Tested.

An excellent example. In Surah Al-Ahzab, the Qur'an uses that phrase for the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. In Surah sixty it uses it again, this time for Ibrahim, Abraham, the friend of God, and those who stood beside him. Being named an example is a heavy honor. People are meant to copy you, and copying is never abstract: it's how you speak, who you stand up to, who you feed. Surah sixty shows two sides of Ibrahim at once, and quietly marks one thing not to copy.

Verse four. Pickthall: "There is a goodly pattern for you in Abraham and those with him". The Arabic is uswa hasana, an excellent example, the same phrase Al-Ahzab uses for the Prophet. Then the verse says what the pattern is. Ibrahim and those with him told their own people, plainly, that they would not worship what their people worshipped besides God. They stood firm, even against their own families. That's one side. The surah, named for a woman who is tested, was revealed at a time of divided loyalties, and it speaks to people torn between faith and family. But the same verse makes one exception: Ibrahim's words to his father, I will ask forgiveness for you, though I have no power to do anything for you against God. The verse sets that promise outside the pattern, and Surah At-Tawbah says Ibrahim later stopped asking forgiveness for his father, once it was clear his father was an enemy to God. Still, the way he spoke is remembered. Surah Maryam keeps the moment: Ibrahim says to his father, peace be upon you, I will ask my Lord to forgive you. Firm in belief, gentle in speech. That's the second side. And elsewhere the Qur'an shows a third: his table. In Surah Adh-Dhariyat, strangers arrive at Ibrahim's door. He doesn't know who they are. He hurries to his family and comes back with a fattened calf. Firm, tender, and quick to feed a stranger. The verse calls the whole pattern beautiful.
screen: `USWA HASANA: AN EXCELLENT EXAMPLE.` · `FIRM WITH HIS PEOPLE.` · `TENDER WITH HIS FATHER.` · `A FATTENED CALF FOR STRANGERS.`

segments.voice: Picture your own door, desk or table, and who might come to it this week: a neighbor, a new colleague, a friend you've lost touch with. Picture Ibrahim hurrying to bring the best he had. Choose one small act of welcome you could offer, a cup of tea, a seat, a warm hello, and hold it in mind.
Ibrahim. In him and those with him, Surah sixty says, is an excellent example: firm in faith, tender with his father, generous at his table. Today's word.
Your line: an excellent example. Firm, tender and generous, all in one person. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslims honor Ibrahim as the friend of God, khalil Allah, and invoke him in every prayer; his hospitality is held up as a model, and Muslim hosts often speak of honoring the guest as a duty of faith.

original.note: Arabic: an excellent example, a beautiful pattern. Used for Ibrahim (60:4, 60:6) and the Prophet (33:21).

trapdoor: what you thought: Ibrahim is an example because he was a great prophet.
what it means: an example of firmness, tenderness and hospitality, all in one person.
what a scholar hears: uswa hasana in 60:4 and 33:21; the exception for Ibrahim's istighfar for his father, read with 19:47 and 9:114; the guests of 51:24–27.

chat.says: What makes Ibrahim an example in Surah sixty? He argued with his own family.
options: He stood firm in belief, yet spoke tenderly to his father and fed strangers.
He cut off his family completely and never spoke kindly to them again.
Everything he did, even asking forgiveness for his father, is the pattern.
chat.meaning: The surah shows him firm with his people and gentle with his father; elsewhere the Qur'an shows him hurrying to feed strangers.

notes: Pickthall wording of 60:4 quoted from memory; please confirm.

60:4 also includes strong words of enmity toward idol worship 'until ye believe in Allah only'; the script summarizes it as Ibrahim telling his people he would not worship what they worshipped. A Keeper may want to adjust.
The claim that uswa hasana is used only for Ibrahim (60:4, 60:6) and the Prophet (33:21) should be confirmed.

Reviewer fix: the earlier draft presented the 60:4 exception (Ibrahim's promise to seek forgiveness for his father) as part of the example to admire. Most classical commentators (e.g. Ibn Kathir, al-Tabari) read it as excluded from the example, read with 9:114. The teach now says so; the tenderness of his speech is drawn from 19:47. Confirm the framing.
